stories.headline: S&P 500 SLIPS 0.28% AS CHIP SELLOFF DEEPENS AHEAD OF NVIDIA EARNINGS
stories.body: The S&P 500 fell 0.28% to 7,652.86 and the Nasdaq 100 dropped 0.80% to 29,075.72 as Micron slid 5.8%, AMD lost more than 3%, and Broadcom fell over 2% on de-risking ahead of Nvidia's earnings Wednesday. The Dow bucked the trend, adding 0.26% to 53,417 as money rotated into consumer defensive names.
stories.explain: Investors often trim a sector's most-correlated names before its bellwether reports, since Nvidia's results function as a read-through for the entire AI capex cycle — a miss or soft guidance there would reprice the whole semiconductor complex, not just Nvidia. That asymmetry, a small position-trimming cost now versus a large repricing risk if Wednesday disappoints, is why chips underperformed a tape that also had tariff and sanctions headlines to digest.

stories.headline: TRUMP HITS CANADA WITH 50% TARIFFS AS TRADE TALKS COLLAPSE
stories.body: The U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods early Saturday after negotiations broke down, with both governments blaming the other. Canadian PM Mark Carney pledged dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs effective Sept. 8.
stories.explain: A tariff is levied on the U.S. importer of record, not the Canadian exporter, so the immediate mechanism is higher input costs passed through to U.S. buyers unless the exporter cuts its price to absorb it — and with Canadian exports like autos, lumber and aluminum already running thin margins, there's little room to absorb a 50% hit. Carney's dollar-for-dollar retaliation is designed to inflict symmetric political pain rather than win on economics, making the tariffs costly enough for Washington that a rollback before Sept. 8 becomes the incentive-compatible outcome.

stories.headline: TREASURY TO UNLEASH 'ECONOMIC D-DAY' SANCTIONS PACKAGE ON IRAN
stories.body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is set to announce Monday what he calls the "single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary," targeting Iran and third parties that do business with it. Iran's currency hit a record low of 2.02 million rial to the dollar as the announcement neared.
stories.explain: Secondary sanctions work by threatening to cut any foreign bank or company that transacts with the sanctioned entity off from the U.S. dollar financial system — since most global trade and reserves are dollar-denominated, that threat alone is usually enough to make third parties stop dealing with Iran even without direct U.S. jurisdiction over them. That extraterritorial reach is why the rial collapsed to a record low before the package was even formally unveiled: markets are pricing the loss of Iran's remaining trade and oil-revenue channels in advance.

stories.headline: MARKETS BRACE FOR WARSH'S FIRST JACKSON HOLE SPEECH FRIDAY
stories.body: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole keynote Friday, 19 days before the Sept. 16 FOMC decision, with this year's symposium theme, "Financial Innovation and Policy," centered on digital payments for the first time. Investors want clarity on his reaction function to a labor market showing cracks alongside inflation that hasn't fully cooled, not a rate signal itself.
stories.explain: A reaction function tells markets how a central banker will respond to future data, not just what they'll do at the next meeting, so a speech emphasizing labor-market softness would raise the implied odds of a September cut and pull yields and the dollar lower, while one stressing sticky inflation would do the opposite. Today's dip in the 10-year to 4.70% alongside a firmer dollar looks like positioning ahead of that binary outcome rather than a directional bet.

stories.headline: OIL SLIDES 2% AS GOLD PUSHES TOWARD $4,650 ON DOLLAR, DEBT WORRIES
stories.body: WTI crude fell 2.15% to $85.19 a barrel even as the Iran sanctions news loomed, while gold rose 0.76% to $4,650.64 an ounce, extending its August rally on persistent concerns about the U.S. debt load and a soft dollar.
stories.explain: Oil and gold are pricing two different risks off the same Iran headline: crude's decline suggests traders see the sanctions package as unlikely to meaningfully cut Iranian supply given historical leakage through intermediaries, while gold's bid reflects a separate, slower-moving trade tied to the $40 trillion U.S. debt load and dollar softness that has little to do with today's specific news. The divergence shows gold currently trading more as a currency-debasement hedge than a pure risk-off asset.

stories.headline: KENTUCKY JUDGE GRANTS ELIGIBILITY TO CASTELLANOS, MITCHELL AS PORTAL FALLOUT CONTINUES
stories.body: A Kentucky judge issued a temporary restraining order making Thomas Castellanos and Mark Mitchell eligible for 2026-27 and free to enter the portal, part of a wave of state-court rulings the NCAA says only protects players who won individual state cases, not those relying solely on the Colorado ruling. Mitchell has already committed to Kentucky, joining fellow eligibility-case transfers Donovan Dent (LSU), Treysen Eaglestaff (UC San Diego) and Dallin Hall (Utah State).

stories.headline: KLAY THOMPSON SIGNS WITH HEAT AFTER MAVERICKS BUYOUT, JOINING GIANNIS AND BAM
stories.body: Miami finalized a two-year, roughly $11.5 million deal with four-time champion Klay Thompson after he cleared waivers following his Mavericks buyout, giving the Heat a second Hall of Fame-caliber addition this summer alongside Giannis Antetokounmpo. Thompson landed on Miami's radar once LeBron James signed instead with Philadelphia earlier this offseason.

stories.headline: BROWNS NAME DESHAUN WATSON WEEK 1 STARTER OVER SHEDEUR SANDERS
stories.body: Cleveland handed Deshaun Watson the Week 1 starting job two days after he was booed by home fans in preseason, setting up his first regular-season start since tearing his Achilles in 2024, an injury he later re-tore. Elsewhere, the Texans traded for receiver Kayshon Boutte from New England to help replace injured Jayden Higgins.

stories.headline: NCAA OVERSIGHT COMMITTEE ADVANCES TRANSFER-WINDOW AND OFFSEASON PRACTICE OVERHAUL
stories.body: The FBS Oversight Committee's proposal to add OTA-style spring practices, two offseason windows totaling 21 practices, heads toward a final August vote, with changes set to take effect Jan. 1, 2027 if approved. The move comes as programs adjust to 2026 being the first cycle without a spring transfer portal window, forcing one-shot roster construction this year.

sports.detail: Fall camp wrapped with a Saturday scrimmage; practices are now closed as the team preps for an unprecedented Labor Day-weekend Apple Cup. QB Demond Williams Jr. made the Maxwell Award watch list. Next: vs. Washington State, Sun. Sept. 6, Husky Stadium (NBC).

Roster filled out at the 15-player max with transfer Harun Zrno (Rutgers) joining fellow portal adds Ryan Beasley (San Francisco), Parker Friedrichsen (Davidson), Steele Venters (Gonzaga) and LeJuan Watts (Texas Tech). Danny Sprinkle also hired longtime NBA assistant Charles Klask to the staff.

Lost to the Titans 19-16 Sunday, a second straight preseason defeat. Rookie safety Bud Clark will miss multiple months with a broken ankle; Drew Lock outplayed Jalen Milroe, who threw a costly interception. NFL owners vote on the Khosla group's $9.6B purchase of the team Wed., Aug. 26, in Atlanta.

The Jalen Duren restricted free agency standoff has turned contentious — Duren declined to address his contract at 'Jalen Duren Day,' and ESPN's Shams Charania says 'both sides are dug in.' The Clippers remain the most-mentioned trade suitor; without a deal, Duren could play on the qualifying offer and reach unrestricted free agency in 2027.

deepDive.title: Tariff Pass-Through: Who Actually Pays a 50% Tariff?
content: Trump's new 50% tariff on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods raises a question that sounds simple but isn't: who actually bears that cost? The answer determines whether the tariff shows up as a modest bump in U.S. inflation data, a squeeze on Canadian exporters' margins, or some blend of both, and it's central to whether tariffs work as effective negotiating leverage or just a tax that ricochets back onto U.S. households. It's also directly relevant to Fed Chair Warsh's read on inflation heading into Friday's Jackson Hole speech, since tariff-driven price increases complicate the case for rate cuts.

Mechanically, a tariff is collected from the U.S. importer of record at the border, not the foreign exporter, so the exporter never writes a check to the U.S. Treasury. What happens next is a question of incidence: the exporter can cut its pre-tariff price to stay competitive, the importer can absorb the cost in its own margin, or the cost can be passed forward to the end consumer through a higher shelf price. Which of these dominates depends on relative elasticities, essentially, whichever side has fewer good alternatives ends up eating more of the cost, because that side has less room to walk away from the transaction.

The 2018-19 U.S.-China tariff episode gives a real answer instead of a theoretical one: multiple Federal Reserve and NBER studies found nearly complete pass-through onto U.S. import prices, with Chinese exporters cutting their own prices only marginally. That happened because Chinese exporters faced elastic, price-sensitive global demand and had little pricing power to protect, while U.S. importers, having already committed to supply chains and product lines, had limited short-run substitutes. The upshot: American firms and consumers, not Chinese producers, absorbed most of that tariff's cost, which is the opposite of what tariff proponents typically promise.

Canada's situation points the same direction, arguably more so. The goods being hit, autos, lumber, aluminum, are commodity-like and already low-margin, meaning Canadian exporters have very little room to cut prices to absorb a 50% tariff without selling at a loss. That points toward high pass-through into U.S. import prices, which is exactly the kind of cost-push pressure that could show up in the CPI's goods components in the months ahead, and exactly the sort of complication Warsh will have to address Friday if he wants to argue that any near-term inflation pickup is transitory rather than something the Fed needs to lean against.
